title: Firestopping
short_answer: A rated wall is only rated if every hole through it and every joint around it is sealed with a tested system — not caulk, a listed system with a number.
summary: A rated wall is only rated if every hole through it and every joint around it is sealed with a tested system. Not caulk — a system, with a number.
plain_words: When you put a hole in a fire wall, or when there's a gap at the top of one, you can't just fill it with whatever's on the truck. There's a tested assembly with a number — it specifies the exact material, how deep, how big the gap is allowed to be, and what backing goes behind it. Build the number that's on the drawings. And photograph it before it gets covered, because afterward there's no way to prove it was right.

steps.body: The system number on the drawings matches the condition actually in front of you — joint type, movement class, and width band.
Annular space measured and within the listed range.
Packing at the specified depth, sealant at the specified depth, correct class.
Labels installed if the spec asks for them.
Photograph every firestop, with the location identified and the system number noted, before anything covers it.
Head-of-wall photographed along its length, not just one spot.
Anything you found that isn't ours — an unsealed penetration by another trade — reported in writing, not quietly fixed.

warnings.title: Why this one is different
warnings.body: Most of our work is judged on how it looks. This is judged on whether a listed system was reproduced exactly, by an inspector, against a document. Close enough is a failure. It's also the item most likely to hold up a certificate of occupancy.

warnings.title: Who firestops the penetrations
warnings.body: "Who firestops the penetrations" is one of the most common scope gaps in commercial interiors — when nobody claims it, it lands on the drywall contractor by default. Get it answered in writing at the job start. If it's ours, it's scope and it gets priced. If it shows up later and it isn't in our contract, see Spotting a Change Order.

warnings.title: Two families — know which is yours
warnings.body: Joint systems (head of wall, wall-to-wall) are ours when we built the partition. Through-penetration firestops are usually the trade that made the hole — confirm on every job.

experts.summary: UL system numbers decode the condition. Joint systems use format XX-Y-NNNN (e.g. HW-D-1000): first pair = joint type (HW head-of-wall, WW wall-to-wall, FW floor-to-wall, FF floor-to-floor); middle letter = movement (D dynamic — joint moves; S static — no movement); number = nominal joint width (0000–0999 up to 2", 1000–1999 over 2" up to 6", 2000–2999 over 6" up to 12"). HW-D-1000 = head-of-wall, dynamic, width over 2" up to 6". Our head-of-wall almost always moves (deflection track) — use a dynamic system; static fill tears on first load. Through-penetrations (e.g. W-L-1087) are specific to the penetrant — a metallic-pipe system is not a cable-bundle system. F rating = hours flame stopped; T rating = unexposed side stays under 325°F above ambient. Many specs require T equal to F on dwelling-unit and patient-room separations — wrong T rating means wrong system even when F matches.

experts.tag: Full detail · installing to the listing
experts.summary: Annular space = gap between penetrant and hole edge; listing gives min and max — inspectors measure it. Packing/backing (usually mineral wool) at specified depth is a tested component, not filler. Fill depth is specified — skinning the surface with a void behind fails when probed. Sealant: intumescent (expands with heat — plastic pipe, cable) vs elastomeric (flexible — metal, moving joints) — not interchangeable. Substrate clean and dry; both sides where the listing says both. Don't overcut the hole — sloppy cutouts are why hole accuracy is on the Hanging checklist. Label each firestop with system number, installer, and date when the spec requires it.

common_mistakes.title: Static system in a dynamic joint
common_mistakes.wrong: Use static firestop at a moving head-of-wall
common_mistakes.right: Dynamic (D) system sized to the actual joint width band
common_mistakes.why: Passes inspection day, tears on first structural load

common_mistakes.title: Annular space out of range
common_mistakes.right: Measure and cut to keep annular space in the listing
common_mistakes.why: Most common field failure after wrong movement class

common_mistakes.title: Underfilled depth
common_mistakes.right: Packing and fill at listed depths

common_mistakes.title: Wrong sealant class
common_mistakes.right: Match sealant class to penetrant and listing

provenance.note: UL numbering (joint type, D/S movement, width bands), F/T rating definitions, and install concepts from UL guide information and International Firestop Council material on ASTM/UL standards; through-penetration systems tested to UL 1479 / ASTM E814, joint systems to UL 2079 / ASTM E1966. The specific listed system on the project drawings governs annular spaces, depths, materials, and cycle counts. Scope ownership of penetration firestopping is contractual — get it in writing at job start.
